results.content:
Problem 2.1 (BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION). Given a signed graph G = (V, E^+ ∪ E^−), find a set 𝒜 = { I_v ⊂ ℝ : v ∈ V } of non-empty, contiguous intervals that maximizes

agree(G, 𝒜) = ∑_{ {u,v} ∈ E^+ } 1(I_u ∩ I_v ≠ ∅) + ∑_{ {u,v} ∈ E^− } 1(I_u ∩ I_v = ∅), (1)

where 1(E) is the indicator function, which takes value 1 if E is true and 0 otherwise.
results.route_rationale: Definition of the objective function; only well-definedness is checkable, no non-trivial assertion to formalise.

fallback_result.reasoning: The objective agree(G,𝒜) is a well-defined finite sum of indicator functions over the disjoint edge sets E^+ and E^−. The definition is used consistently throughout the paper. No algebraic or logical error.

results.content: Relationship to CORRELATION CLUSTERING. First, consider any CORRELATION CLUSTERING solution C1, …, Ck, and consider k non-overlapping intervals I1, …, Ik. Now we assign each vertex in Ci to the same interval Ii. Thus, if u, v ∈ Ci, then their intervals overlap, and, if u ∈ Ci and v ∈ Cj for i ≠ j, then their intervals do not overlap. This implies that the optimal solution of BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION will always yield an agreement at least as large as for CORRELATION CLUSTERING.
results.route_rationale: Constructive expressivity argument that depends on CORRELATION CLUSTERING definitions; informal review is sufficient.

fallback_result.reasoning: The argument is sound. Any CC partition C_1,…,C_k can be embedded by assigning k pairwise-disjoint non-empty intervals (e.g. I_i = [i, i+1/2]) to the clusters. Positive edges within a cluster then overlap and negative edges across clusters are disjoint, so the BIA objective of this assignment equals the CC objective (positive-within plus negative-between); hence OPT_BIA ≥ OPT_CC. No error.

results.content: Second, our interval representation is strictly more expressive and, for instance, allows us to model non-transitive node relationships and this property is illustrated in Figure 2. This is neither possible in CORRELATION CLUSTERING nor in the structural balance theory of Harary [28], in both of which no cycle with exactly one negative edge can be represented without error.
results.route_rationale: Existential interval-construction claim (a triangle with one negative edge is interval-representable); formalisable and machine-checkable.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the existential interval representation of a triangle with one negative edge: there exist non-empty closed real intervals A, B, C with A∩B≠∅, B∩C≠∅, A∩C=∅. Lean proved the claim with the witness A=Icc 0 1, B=Icc (1/2) (3/2), C=Icc (3/2) 2 (A∩C empty since 1 < 3/2). The CC/structural-balance impossibility side (an unbalanced triangle cannot be partitioned) is classical and was checked informally.

results.location: 2 Problem Definition and Theoretical Results (Relationship to Interval Editing)
results.content: The case of complete graphs and relationship to Interval Editing. If G is a complete signed graph then it can be represented without error in BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION if and only if G^+ = (V, E^+) is an interval graph. That is because missing edges in G^+ correspond to negative edges in G (since G is complete). Thus, making the minimum number of edge deletions/insertions to turn G^+ into an interval graph is equivalent to flipping the minimum number of edge signs in G such that we have agreement for all edges.
results.route_rationale: Characterisation theorem requiring interval-graph theory; a faithful Lean formalisation is too large for a proof budget.

fallback_result.reasoning: The iff is correct. If G is complete and admits a conflict-free representation, then for every pair {u,v}, I_u∩I_v≠∅ iff {u,v}∈E^+ (a missing positive edge is a negative edge, which requires disjointness), so G^+ is exactly the interval graph of {I_v}. Conversely, any interval representation of G^+ makes non-adjacent vertices have disjoint intervals, which satisfies the negative edges of G. The Interval Editing equivalence (flipping minimum signs = minimum interval-editing distance of G^+) is standard. No error.

results.content:
Theorem 2.2 (Revised). We provide a construction mapping instances of ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION to BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION; however, the interval assignments encoding acyclic partitions rely on strict ordering assumptions that do not hold in all interval configurations. Consequently, the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction, pending a corrected reduction.

The theorem has several implications for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION in incomplete graphs: (1) The disagreement version is hard to approximate within any factor. (2) It is not FPT when parameterized by the number of required edge deletions (unless P = NP), separating it from the problem in complete graphs. (3) The result holds even when restricted to graphs G = (V', E^+ ∪ E^-) where G^+ = (V', E^+) is a chordless cycle. This is intriguing because many algorithmic results on interval graphs rely on detecting forbidden induced subgraphs like chordless cycles of four or more vertices [10, 63, 36]. Our hardness result implies that detecting these forbidden structures is NP-hard for incomplete signed graphs.

We prove Theorem 2.2 in Appendix A, where we construct a new graph G from an ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION instance H, and show that G can be represented conflict-free if and only if H is a YES-instance.
results.route_rationale: Meta-statement about a reduction's validity; the load-bearing check is internal consistency of the theorem with the manuscript's own proof and claims, done informally.

fallback_result.reasoning: Internal contradiction in the manuscript's mathematical claims. Theorem 2.2 (Revised) asserts the ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION reduction 'does not guarantee an equivalence' and that 'the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open'. But (i) the Introduction states 'we show that BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION is NP-hard even when the graph G^+ = (V, E^+) induced by the positive edges forms a cycle'; (ii) the paragraph immediately below the theorem lists implications (1)-(3) that only follow from an established NP-hardness result; and (iii) Appendix A.3 is titled 'Proof of Theorem 2.2' and proves the equivalence in both directions ('We first show that if H=(V,E) is a YES-instance ... then the constructed signed graph instance G has a conflict-free interval-representation' and 'Conversely, suppose the constructed instance G admits a conflict-free interval representation ... this implies H is a YES-instance'). These assertions are mutually inconsistent — the theorem cannot simultaneously be an open problem, an established result with consequences, and a proved theorem. The manuscript offers no resolution.

results.location: 2.2 A PTAS for fixed k in complete graphs
results.content: Theorem 2.3. Let G be a complete signed graph and let ε > 0, δ > 0 and k ∈ N be parameters. There exists an algorithm that, with probability at least 1 − δ, returns a (1 + ε)-approximate solution for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION when the algorithm can only use k different intervals and it runs in time 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(εδ))/ε^3)} · n.
results.route_rationale: Running-time enumeration bound in the theorem's proof is a concrete counting claim; formalisable in Lean.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the enumeration bound used in the proof of Theorem 2.3: an overlap pattern of k intervals is a Boolean choice per unordered pair of distinct intervals, and the number of such patterns is exactly 2^{k(k−1)/2} (equivalently 2^{binom(k,2)}), the 'at most 2^{binom(k,2)}' claim of the proof. The theorem's running-time arithmetic 2^{O(k^2 + (1/ε^3) log(k) log(k/(εδ)))}·n ≤ 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(εδ))/ε^3)}·n is consistent in the ε→0 regime. The full probabilistic PTAS claim was reviewed informally (see summary); a separate section-level inconsistency is reported under THEOREM::5.

results.location: 2.2 A PTAS for fixed k in complete graphs
results.content: We attempt to solve the generalized CORRELATION CLUSTERING problem by partitioning V into m based on random sampling but acknowledge that overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies making greedy assignments approximate at best. The complexity of enumerating assignments grows exponentially with the number of overlapping cluster combinations, which may be prohibitively large. Due to these challenges, while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.
results.route_rationale: Feasibility claim whose consistency with Theorem 2.3 and Appendix B is the load-bearing check; done informally.

fallback_result.reasoning: Internal contradiction. This paragraph states that 'while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods' — i.e. that no general fixed-k PTAS is available with current methods. But Theorem 2.3 (same section) asserts the existence of a (1+ε)-PTAS for the general fixed-k complete-graph setting with running time 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(εδ))/ε^3)}·n, and Appendix B proves it via Proposition B.1 and Corollary B.2. The paragraph directly denies the theorem that the same section states and proves. At most one of the two can be correct; the manuscript gives no indication which.

results.content:
Lemma A.1. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that for all u ∈ V′ \ {S}: r(IS) < r(Iu), and for all u ∈ V′ \ {T}: ℓ(Iu) < ℓ(IT).

Proof. Towards a contradiction assume there exists a vertex u ∈ V′ \ {S} such that r(Iu) ≤ r(IS). As (V′, E+) is a cycle, there exists a path from u to T that does not include S. The union Ip of the intervals corresponding to the vertices in this path must form an interval itself. As r(Iu) ≤ r(IS), but ℓ(IT) > r(IS), IS ∩ Ip ≠ ∅, and consequently there exists some vertex x ∈ V′ \ {S}, x ≠ u along this path such that IS ∩ Ix ≠ ∅. Note that by the construction of this path, x cannot be a positive neighbor of S, as we explicitly choose one of the two paths from u to T that does not include S. Then, {S, x} ∈ E−, leading to a contradiction. Finally, for all u ∈ V′ \ {T}: ℓ(Iu) < ℓ(IT) holds by a symmetric argument.
results.route_rationale: Interval + graph geometry over the full reduction construction; a faithful Lean formalisation is too large for a proof budget.

fallback_result.reasoning: The statement is true. The proof's 'x ≠ u' step is under-justified when u is a positive neighbour of S (u ∈ {L, H_S}), but the claim still holds under the full constraint set: the path S–L–M–R–T with {S,M},{S,R},{S,T},{L,R},{M,T} ∈ E^−, the disjointness chain, and the WLOG assumption r(I_S) < ℓ(I_T) force every interval except I_S to extend strictly to the right of r(I_S) (otherwise I_R or I_T would have to overlap I_S); the T-side is symmetric. No false claim; only a presentation gap.

results.content:
Lemma A.2. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that (i) for all u ∈ V′ \ {S, L, HS}: r(IS) < ℓ(Iu), and (ii) for all u ∈ V′ \ {T, R, HT}: r(Iu) < ℓ(IT).

Proof. Assume towards a contradiction that there exists a vertex u ∈ V′ \ {S, L, HS} such that ℓ(Iu) ≤ r(IS). From Lemma A.1, we know r(Iu) > r(IS), so it follows that Iu ∩ IS ≠ ∅. However, since {S, u} ∈ E− this leads to a contradiction with the assumption of a conflict-free interval representation. The proof for (ii) follows symmetrically.
results.route_rationale: Interval + graph geometry; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. For u ∉ {S,L,H_S}, the construction gives {S,u} ∈ E^− (E^-_S connects S to every vertex except L and H_S). If ℓ(I_u) ≤ r(I_S), then Lemma A.1 (r(I_u) > r(I_S)) implies I_u ∩ I_S ≠ ∅ (both are closed intervals with r(I_S) ∈ I_S and r(I_S) ∈ I_u), contradicting the negative edge. Symmetric for T. No error.

results.content:
Lemma A.3. For any conflict-free interval representation of G, it must hold that for all v ∈ V: IMv ⊂ IM.

Proof. By construction, the open interval (r(IS), ℓ(IT)) ⊂ IL ∪ IM ∪ IR. From Lemma A.2, we know that IMv ⊂ IL ∪ IM ∪ IR. Finally, as {Mv, L}, {Mv, R} ∈ E−, the claim holds.
results.route_rationale: Interval + graph geometry; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. (r(I_S), ℓ(I_T)) ⊂ I_L ∪ I_M ∪ I_R follows because the union of the path intervals I_S, I_L, I_M, I_R, I_T is a connected interval covering the open gap (consecutive positive edges make the union an interval, and I_S, I_T cannot cover points beyond their own endpoints). Lemma A.2 puts I_{M_v} inside the gap; {M_v, L}, {M_v, R} ∈ E^− exclude I_L and I_R, so I_{M_v} ⊂ I_M. No error.

results.content:
Lemma A.4. For any conflict-free interval representation of G, it must hold that for all v ∈ V either IXv ⊂ IL or IXv ⊂ IR but not both.

Proof. By construction, the open interval (r(IS), ℓ(IT)) ⊂ IL ∪ IM ∪ IR. From Lemma A.2, we know that IXv ⊂ IL ∪ IM ∪ IR. Furthermore, we know that IL ∩ IR = ∅. Finally, as {Xv, M} ∈ E− the claim holds.
results.route_rationale: Interval + graph geometry; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. I_{X_v} lies in (r(I_S), ℓ(I_T)) ⊂ I_L ∪ I_M ∪ I_R by the same union-of-path-intervals argument used in Lemma A.3; I_L ∩ I_R = ∅ ({L,R} ∈ E^-_c); and {X_v, M} ∈ E^-_* excludes I_M, so I_{X_v} is contained in exactly one of I_L, I_R. No error.

results.content:
Lemma A.5. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that for all edges (u, v) ∈ E if IXu ⊂ IR and IXv ⊂ IR, then r(IXu) < ℓ(IXv), and, symmetrically, if IXu ⊂ IL and IXv ⊂ IL, then r(IXv) < ℓ(IXu).

Proof. As we assumed that r(IS) < ℓ(IT), it follows that ℓ(IM) < ℓ(IR) ≤ r(IM) < r(IR). Towards a contradiction, assume there exists an edge (u, v) ∈ E such that IXu ⊂ IR and IXv ⊂ IR, but ℓ(IXv) ≤ r(IXu). As in any conflict-free interval representation, the intervals IXu and IXv are disjoint, this implies that r(IXv) < ℓ(IXu). Now, consider the intervals IMu and IAu. From Lemma A.3, we know that IMu ⊂ IM, hence r(IMu) < ℓ(IXv) < r(IXv) < ℓ(IXu). By construction, IAu must overlap with IMu and IXu, hence ℓ(IAu) ≤ r(IMu) and r(IAu) ≥ ℓ(IXu). However, this implies that IAu ∩ IXv ≠ ∅, leading to a violation of the {Xv, Au} constraint introduced in EE^-.
results.route_rationale: Interval + graph geometry; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: The statement is true. The proof's step 'r(I_{M_u}) < ℓ(I_{X_v})' is asserted from Lemma A.3 alone but additionally uses {X_v, M} ∈ E^-_* (so I_{X_v} ∩ I_M = ∅) and the ordering facts ℓ(I_M) < ℓ(I_R) ≤ r(I_M) < r(I_R) derived from the disjointness chain; together they force I_{X_v} to lie strictly right of I_M, so r(I_{M_u}) ≤ r(I_M) < ℓ(I_{X_v}). With ℓ(I_{X_v}) ≤ r(I_{X_u}) and disjointness giving r(I_{X_v}) < ℓ(I_{X_u}), the overlap conditions ℓ(I_{A_u}) ≤ r(I_{M_u}) and r(I_{A_u}) ≥ ℓ(I_{X_u}) make I_{A_u} ∩ I_{X_v} ≠ ∅, contradicting {X_v, A_u} ∈ E^-_E. The claim is correct; the written proof omits one justification.

Corollary B.2. Let ε > 0 and δ > 0. There exists an algorithm that computes a (1 + ε)-approximate solution for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION with k given intervals in time k^{O(1/ε^3 log(k/(εδ)))} · n with probability at least 1 − δ.

Proof. First, assume that all pairs of intervals overlap. Then it does not matter how we assign the vertices because only the positive edges can be satisfied. In this case, any assignment will achieve the same objective function value as OPT. Second, assume that there is at least one pair of non-overlapping intervals. In that case, we know from CORRELATION CLUSTERING that the objective function agreement must be Ω(n^2) ... we can use the result from Proposition B.1 to obtain a multiplicative (1 + ε)-approximation by making the parameter ε in our additive approximation small enough.
results.route_rationale: Follows from Proposition B.1; the two-case argument is informal-checkable.

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. If all k intervals pairwise overlap, every edge pair overlaps regardless of the assignment, so only positive edges are satisfiable and every assignment attains |E^+| = OPT. Otherwise the optimum agreement is Ω(n²): a one-cluster assignment already yields at least max(|E^+|, |E^-|) ≥ (n choose 2)/2 = Ω(n²), so the additive ε' n²/2 bound of Proposition B.1 with ε' chosen as Ω(ε) yields ALG ≥ OPT − (ε/2)OPT = (1−ε/2)OPT, i.e. a (1+ε)-approximation. No error.

results.location: B A PTAS for a Fixed Number of Intervals
results.content: Proof of Theorem 2.3. Note that we only need to consider at most 2^{\binom{k}{2}} choices for picking k intervals (up to changing their coordinates): For any pair of intervals they either overlap or they do not. Thus, since there are \binom{k}{2} interval pairs, there are at most 2^{\binom{k}{2}} = 2^{O(k^2)} choices for the overlap. Now we can just enumerate all possible overlap-patterns of k intervals and run the algorithm from Corollary B.2 for it in time 2^{O(k^2 + (1/ε^3) log(k) log(k/(εδ)))} · n ≤ 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(εδ))/ε^3)} · n. ... we do not have to apply a union bound that the algorithm succeeds for all possible choices of 2^{O(k^2)} choices of intervals.
results.route_rationale: big-O running-time argument and enumeration bound; the counting sub-claim is verified in Lean (THEOREM::4).

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. The enumeration bound 'at most 2^{\binom{k}{2}} overlap patterns' is exactly the claim verified in Lean (see THEOREM::4): each unordered pair of distinct intervals contributes one Boolean choice, and there are k(k−1)/2 such pairs. The running-time inequality 2^{O(k² + (1/ε³)log(k)log(k/(εδ)))}·n ≤ 2^{O(k²log(k/(εδ))/ε³)}·n holds in the ε→0 regime (k² is absorbed by k²log(k/(εδ))/ε³ since log(k/(εδ)) → ∞ and ε³ → 0). The success-probability argument (only OPT's pattern needs to succeed, so no union bound over all 2^{O(k²)} patterns) is correct.

Lemma B.4. For i = 0, …, m it holds that agree(G, Hi+1) ≥ agree(G, OPT) − i · (1/8)ε^2 n^2.

Proof. ... [derivation bounding the per-vertex loss by 4·(ε/32)|V \ Vi| + 0 ≤ (ε/8)n] ... Thus we get that for all vertices in Vi satisfying Equation (2) we get that their total difference is at most (ε/8)n·|Vi| = ε^2 n^2/32. Furthermore, as there are at most (ε/8)|Vi| vertices that do not satisfy Equation (2), they can contribute at most (ε/8)|Vi|·n = ε^2 n^2/32 edges that are in disagreement. The number of disagreements within Vi is at most |Vi|^2 = ε^2 n^2/16. In total, we get that we have introduced ε^2 n^2/8 new disagreements due to our approximations in the i-th iteration. The lemma now follows by induction.
results.route_rationale: Agreement-loss arithmetic; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: The per-iteration loss decomposition is correct. The algorithm's greedy choice gives agree(u,ℓ,(S)) ≥ agree(u,ℓ',(S)), so the algebraic manipulation in the derivation (adding and subtracting α_i·agree(S) terms) bounds the loss for each good vertex u by 4·(ε/32)|V\V_i| ≤ (ε/8)n. Good vertices: ≤ |V_i|(ε/8)n = (εn/4)(εn/8) = ε²n²/32. Bad vertices (≤ (ε/8)|V_i|): ≤ (ε/8)|V_i|·n = ε²n²/32. Within-V_i edges: |V_i|² = (εn/4)² = ε²n²/16. Total ε²n²/32 + ε²n²/32 + ε²n²/16 = ε²n²/8 (double-counting of within-V_i edges only makes the bound looser). With m = 4/ε iterations the accumulated error is m·ε²n²/8 = εn²/2, matching Proposition B.1. No error.

results.content: Proof of Proposition B.1. The approximation ratio follows from the previous lemma. The running time follows from the fact that there are k^s = k^{O(1/ε^2 log(k/(εδ)))} choices to assign the s vertices in each Si to the k intervals and we have to consider the combinations of these assignments for m = O(1/ε) sets. Thus, the outer loop iterates over k^{ms} = k^{O(1/ε^3 log(k/(εδ)))} assignments. Furthermore, each loop iteration can be implemented in time O(ns).
results.route_rationale: Runtime counting; informal review.

fallback_result.reasoning: Correct. There are k^s assignments of the s sampled vertices of each S_i to the k intervals; with m = 4/ε sets the outer loop enumerates k^{ms} assignments, and ms = (4/ε)·(32²/ε²)log(64mk/(εδ)) = O(1/ε³ log(k/(εδ))), matching k^{O(1/ε³ log(k/(εδ)))}. Each iteration is O(ns). No error.

findings.evidence: Theorem 2.2 (Revised) declares the reduction invalid and the NP-hardness claim open, while the same manuscript proves the equivalence in both directions and asserts NP-hardness as established. Evidence: (a) Theorem statement: 'Consequently, the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction, pending a corrected reduction.' (b) Appendix A.3 'Proof of Theorem 2.2' proves both directions: 'We first show that if $H=(V,E)$ is a YES-instance ... then the constructed signed graph instance $G$ has a conflict-free interval-representation' and 'Conversely ... this implies $H$ is a YES-instance'. (c) Introduction: 'we show that BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION is NP-hard even when the graph $G^+ = (V, E^+)$ induced by the positive edges forms a cycle.' (d) Section 2.1: 'The theorem has several implications ... (1) The disagreement version is hard to approximate within any factor. (2) It is not FPT when parameterized by the number of required edge deletions ...'. These cannot all be true; the paper gives no resolution. An independent informal review of the Appendix A construction (lemmas A.1–A.5, FORMULA_BLOCK::0, PROOF::0) found it internally consistent, which suggests the 'Revised' retraction statement itself is the erroneous element.
findings.exact_quote: Theorem 2.2 (Revised). We provide a construction mapping instances of ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION to BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION; however, the interval assignments encoding acyclic partitions rely on strict ordering assumptions that do not hold in all interval configurations. Consequently, the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction, pending a corrected reduction.

findings.evidence: Section 2.2 states 'while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods', directly denying Theorem 2.3 of the same section, which asserts a (1+ε)-PTAS for the general fixed-k complete-graph setting with running time $2^{O(k^2 \log(k/(\varepsilon\delta))/\varepsilon^3)} \cdot n$, and which Appendix B proves via Proposition B.1 and Corollary B.2. The two statements cannot both be correct; the paper gives no indication which is authoritative.
findings.exact_quote: We attempt to solve the generalized CORRELATION CLUSTERING problem by partitioning V into m based on random sampling but acknowledge that overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies making greedy assignments approximate at best. The complexity of enumerating assignments grows exponentially with the number of overlapping cluster combinations, which may be prohibitively large. Due to these challenges, while a PTAS is feasible for limited and well-structured interval overlaps, the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.

summary: Checked 24 mathematical objects from 'Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs' (signed-graph opinion-interval problem: NP-hardness reduction in Appendix A, PTAS for fixed k in Appendix B, heuristic definitions, and the construction arithmetic). Lean 4 (shared project MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper, kept) formally verified 4 claims, all PASSED: (1) a triangle with exactly one negative edge admits an exact interval representation (∃ closed intervals A,B,C with A∩B≠∅, B∩C≠∅, A∩C=∅); (2) the V1-side X-intervals of the Appendix A.3 construction are pairwise disjoint (0.4 − 2j/(16k) < 0.4 − (2i+1)/(16k) for i<j), the load-bearing arithmetic for the negative-edge set E_V^-; (3) the Chernoff tail bound 2·exp(−2(ε/32)²s) < εδ/(32mk) for s = (32²/ε²)log(64mk/(εδ)) — the quantitative core of Lemma B.3; (4) the number of overlap patterns of k intervals is exactly 2^{k(k−1)/2} — the enumeration bound in the proof of Theorem 2.3. All other concrete mathematics reviewed informally was found sound: the objective (Eq. 1), the expressivity argument, the complete-graph/interval-graph iff, the structural lemmas A.1–A.5, the construction's containment claims, the additive-error arithmetic of Lemma B.4/Proposition B.1, and Corollary B.2's two-case argument. Two CRITICAL internal contradictions were found in the manuscript's mathematical claims, both present in the text with no resolution: (a) Theorem 2.2 (Revised) declares the ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION reduction invalid and the NP-hardness claim open, yet the Introduction, the implications paragraph in Section 2.1, and the Conclusion assert NP-hardness as an established result, and Appendix A.3 proves the equivalence in both directions — the reduction's internal content was found consistent, so the retraction itself appears to be the erroneous element, but regardless the manuscript is self-contradictory; (b) Section 2.2's hedged paragraph states the general fixed-k PTAS is beyond current methods, directly contradicting Theorem 2.3 and its Appendix B proof. Minor observations (not findings): Lemma A.1's proof under-justifies the u ∈ {L, H_S} case and Lemma A.5's proof omits the {X_v, M} justification (the statements hold); Lemma B.3's proof writes '1 − δ/(4mk)' where the computation gives '1 − δ/(4m)' (typo, no effect on the lemma). No Lean result FAILED, so no fallback reviews were required.
